title: The Deadly Poppy Field, part 5
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: They now came upon more and more of the big scarlet poppies, and fewer and fewer of the other flowers; and soon they found themselves in the midst of a great meadow of poppies. Now it is well known that when there are many of these flowers together their odor is so powerful that anyone who breathes it falls asleep, and if the sleeper is not carried away from the scent of the flowers, he sleeps on and on forever. But Dorothy did not know this, nor could she get away from the bright red flowers that were everywhere about; so presently her eyes grew heavy and she felt she must sit down to rest and to sleep.
But the Tin Woodman would not let her do this.

“We must hurry and get back to the road of yellow brick before dark,” he said; and the Scarecrow agreed with him. So they kept walking until Dorothy could stand no longer. Her eyes closed in spite of herself and she forgot where she was and fell among the poppies, fast asleep.
“What shall we do?” asked the Tin Woodman.
“If we leave her here she will die,” said the Lion. “The smell of the flowers is killing us all. I myself can scarcely keep my eyes open, and the dog is asleep already.”
It was true; Toto had fallen down beside his little mistress. But the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, not being made of flesh, were not troubled by the scent of the flowers.

“Run fast,” said the Scarecrow to the Lion, “and get out of this deadly flower bed as soon as you can. We will bring the little girl with us, but if you should fall asleep you are too big to be carried.”
So the Lion aroused himself and bounded forward as fast as he could go. In a moment he was out of sight.

“Let us make a chair with our hands and carry her,” said the Scarecrow. So they picked up Toto and put the dog in Dorothy’s lap, and then they made a chair with their hands for the seat and their arms for the arms and carried the sleeping girl between them through the flowers.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to anyone who breathes the poppies' odour?
options: They fall asleep
They grow suddenly strong
They lose their memory
They begin to weep

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what happens if a sleeper is not carried away from the scent?
options: He sleeps on and on forever
He wakes again by morning
He is poisoned within the hour
He wanders off in his sleep

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who fell asleep before Dorothy?
options: Toto
The Lion
The Scarecrow
Nobody

questions.prompt: Per the passage, why were the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman unharmed?
options: They are not made of flesh
They held their breath the whole way
They walked at the edge of the field
They had no noses to smell with

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Scarecrow tell the Lion to do?
options: Run fast and get out of the flower bed
Carry Dorothy on his back to safety
Lie down and hold his breath
Go back the way they had come

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did Dorothy not avoid the danger?
options: She did not know what the flowers could do
She refused to listen to the Tin Woodman
She had stopped to gather them in her basket
She was too tired to walk any faster

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the Lion sent ahead rather than carried?
options: He is far too big for the others to carry
He can run faster than any of them
He alone knows the way out of the field
He is the only one still fully awake

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did the two of them carry Dorothy?
options: They made a chair of their hands and arms
They dragged her along by the shoulders
They laid her on the Lion's broad back
They took turns carrying her in their arms

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that Dorothy's eyes closed in spite of herself?
options: She could not keep them open however she tried
She shut them deliberately to rest a moment
She was pretending to sleep to stop the walk
She had been told to close them by the Woodman

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: A beautiful meadow turns out to be a slow and deadly trap
A meadow of flowers restores the tired travellers
The Lion abandons the party at the first sign of danger
Dorothy insists on resting against her friends' advice

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Tin Woodman urge as Dorothy grew sleepy?
options: That they hurry back to the road before dark
That she rest for a few minutes only
That the Lion carry her the rest of the way
That they turn back to the riverbank

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Lion say about his own eyes?
options: That he could scarcely keep them open
That the flowers had blinded him
That he saw better than the others
That he would close them and rest

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where was Toto put while Dorothy was carried?
options: In Dorothy's lap
On the Lion's back
In the Scarecrow's arms
In the basket

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what changed about the flowers as they walked on?
options: The scarlet poppies crowded out the other kinds
The flowers grew shorter and more scattered
The scent grew weaker the further they went
The poppies gave way to open grass

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what would happen if Dorothy were left where she fell?
options: She would die there among the flowers
She would wake by herself in the morning
The Lion would carry her out later
The scent would soon wear off her

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Lion aroused himself?
options: Stirred himself into action
Woke up from a deep sleep
Grew angry at the Scarecrow
Roared to clear his head

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarises the passage?
options: Those who cannot fall asleep save the ones who can
The whole party falls asleep among the poppies
The Lion carries Dorothy clear of the flowers
Dorothy wakes in time to warn her friends
